'''Joseph Liouville''' ({{IPAc-en|ˌ|l|i:|u|ˈ|v|ɪ|l}} {{respell|LEE|oo|VIL}}; {{IPA|fr|ʒozɛf ljuvil|lang}}; 24 March 1809 – 8 September 1882)<ref>His death is registered the 9th of Septembre [http://archives.paris.fr/arkotheque/visionneuse/visionneuse.php?arko=YTo2OntzOjQ6ImRhdGUiO3M6MTA6IjIwMTgtMDUtMDYiO3M6MTA6InR5cGVfZm9uZHMiO3M6MTE6ImFya29fc2VyaWVsIjtzOjQ6InJlZjEiO2k6NztzOjQ6InJlZjIiO2k6MzYxNDtzOjE2OiJ2aXNpb25uZXVzZV9odG1sIjtiOjE7czoyMToidmlzaW9ubmV1c2VfaHRtbF9tb2RlIjtzOjQ6InByb2QiO30=#uielem_move=1%2C-812&uielem_islocked=0&uielem_zoom=132&uielem_brightness=0&uielem_contrast=0&uielem_isinverted=0&uielem_rotate=F Etat civil de la ville de Paris, 6ème arrondissement].</ref><ref>[http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k278320w/f1.item.r=Liouville.zoom Figaro du 10 décembre 1882]</ref> was a French mathematician who worked on a number of different fields in mathematics, including [[number theory]], [[complex analysis]], and [[mathematical physics]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Smithies |first=Frank |date=October 1991 |title=''Joseph Liouville 1809-1882: Master of Pure and Applied Mathematics'', by Jesper Lützen |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-gazette/article/abs/joseph-liouville-18091882-master-of-pure-and-applied-mathematics-by-jesper-lutzen-pp-884-dm228-1990-isbn-3540971807-springer/F6239135C428B659D48D60768417A5F9 |journal=[[The Mathematical Gazette]] |volume=75 |issue=473 |pages=372-3 |doi=10.2307/3619531|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Many mathematical concepts are named after him, including [[Liouville's theorem (Hamiltonian)|Liouville's theorem in Hamiltonian mechanics]] and [[Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)|Liouville's theorem for complex numbers]].

== Life and work ==
He was born in [[Saint-Omer, Pas-de-Calais|Saint-Omer]] in France on 24 March 1809.<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|access-date=2017-04-28|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074135/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Joseph Liouville {{!}} French mathematician {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joseph-Liouville|access-date=2021-12-11|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}}</ref> His parents were Claude-Joseph Liouville (an army officer) and Thérèse Liouville (née Balland).

Liouville gained admission to the [[École Polytechnique]] in 1825 and graduated in 1827. Just like [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]] before him, Liouville studied engineering at [[École des Ponts et Chaussées]] after graduating from the Polytechnique, but opted instead for a career in mathematics.<ref name=":0" /> After some years as an assistant at various institutions including the [[École Centrale Paris]], he was appointed as professor at the École Polytechnique in 1838. He began delivering lectures on mathematics at the [[Collège de France]] in 1851 secured a chair in [[Classical mechanics|rational mechanics]] at the Faculté des Sciences in 1857. However, he suffered under a heavy teaching load and his health started to deteriorate.<ref name=":0" />

Liouville founded the ''[[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]]'' in 1836, basing it on ''[[Crelle's Journal]]''. It soon became a leading mathematical periodical in France and became known as "Liouville's Journal" even after he had resigned as editor-in-chief in 1875.<ref name=":0" /> He was elected to the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in 1839, and became an associate member of the [[Bureau des Longitudes]].<ref name=":0" />

Liouville was also involved in politics for some time, and he became a member of the [[National Assembly of France|Constituting Assembly]] in following the [[French Revolution of 1848|1848 Revolution]]. However, following the rise of [[Napoleon III]] to power, Liouville ended his political activities.<ref name=":0" />

In 1851, he was elected a foreign member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]]. In 1853, he was elected as a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?year=1853;year-max=1853;smode=advanced;startDoc=1|access-date=2021-04-16|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> As a mathematician, he maintained contact with many foreign colleagues, including William Thomson ([[Lord Kelvin]]), [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]], and [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]].<ref name=":0" /> As a lecturer, he offered support and encouragement to many young talents, among them, [[Charles Hermite]], [[Joseph Bertrand]], and [[Joseph-Alfred Serret]].<ref name=":0" />

== Contributions ==

=== Analysis, algebra, and number theory ===
[[File:Journal math liouville.jpg|thumb|right|Title page of the first volume of ''Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées'' in 1836.]]
In 1835, Liouville established the existence of [[Nonelementary integral|non-elementary integrals]] and [[Liouville's theorem (differential algebra)|a criterion]] for integration in finite terms, that is, in terms of [[Elementary function|elementary functions]].<ref name=":0" /> He gave an example of such a non-elementary integral, <math>\int \frac{e^x}{x} \, dx</math>.<ref name=":3">{{cite book|title=The Calculus Gallery|first=William|last=Dunham|isbn=978-0-691-13626-4|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2005|page=|author-link=William Dunham (mathematician)}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=119}}

In 1838, Liouville published a method for establishing the existence of solutions to [[Ordinary differential equation|ordinary differential equations]] of the second order involving successive approximations, now attached to the name of [[Émile Picard]], who gave [[Picard's Method|a more general approach]] in the early 1890s.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|pages=719-20}}

In algebra, Liouville was one of the first to grasp the significance of the contributions of the late [[Évariste Galois]], whose work had been forwarded to him by Auguste Chevalier, a friend of Galois.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ehrhardt |first=Caroline |date=August 2011 |title=A quarrel between Joseph Liouville and Guillaume Libri at the French Academy of Sciences in the middle of the nineteenth century |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S031508601100005X |journal=[[Historia Mathematica]] |volume=38 |issue=3 |pages=389-414 |doi=10.1016/j.hm.2011.02.002|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Liouville edited and published the work of Galois in his own journal in 1846, after which the [[Galois theory]] attracted the attention of many mathematicians, among them, [[Paolo Ruffini]], [[Joseph-Alfred Serret]], and [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]].<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=766}} By helping to popularize the works of Galois, Liouville participated, albeit indirectly, in the development of [[Abstract algebra|modern algebra]] in general and [[group theory]] in particular.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Taton|first=René|author-link=René Taton|title=[[Dictionary of Scientific Biography]]|publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons|year=1970–1980|editor-last=Gillispie|editor-first=Charles Coulston|editor-link=Charles Coulston Gillispie|location=New York|at=Joseph Liouville}}</ref>

Research on the solutions of algebraic equations spurred interest in [[Algebraic number|algebraic]] and transcendental [[Irrational number|irrational numbers]].<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=980}} In 1844,<ref>{{cite journal <!--DUPLICATE| url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb343481087/date1844.liste--> | url=http://www.bibnum.education.fr/mathematiques/theorie-des-nombres/propos-de-l-existence-des-nombres-transcendants | author=Joseph Liouville | title=Mémoires et communications | journal=[[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences]] | volume=18 | number=20,21 | pages=883&ndash;885,910&ndash;911 | date=May 1844 | language=French}}</ref> Liouville was the first to prove the existence of [[transcendental number]]s. He did so by demonstrating some results on approximating algebraic irrationals using rational numbers and established [[Liouville number|an inequality]] that served as a criterion for transcendence.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=981}} In essence, his inequality proclaims that rationals are poor approximations of irrational algebraic numbers.<ref name=":3" />{{Reference page|page=124}} He then gave an explicit example. He showed that any number of the form 

<math>\frac{a_1}{10} + \frac{a_2}{10^{2!}} + \frac{a_3}{10^{3!}} + \cdots,</math> 

where the <math>a_i</math> are integers from 0 to 9, is transcendental.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=981}} Future demonstrations of the transcendence of [[E (mathematical constant)|Euler's number]] <math>e</math> by Charles Hermite and of <math>\pi</math> ([[pi]]) by [[Ferdinand von Lindemann]] were based on Liouville's contributions.<ref name=":3" />{{Reference page|page=127}} 

The [[Liouville function]], an important concept in number theory, is named in his honor. 

In his work on [[Elliptic integral|elliptic integrals]], he based the whole subject on the general properties of [[Doubly periodic function|doubly periodic functions]] and he demonstrated the [[Transcendental number|transcendence]] of [[Abelian integral|Abelian functions]].<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=650}} It was in this context that he discovered [[Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)|Liouville's theorem]] in complex analysis, bounded [[Entire function|entire functions]] are constant.<ref name=":0" /> He also gave a short proof of the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]].<ref name=":5" />

A similar result is Liouville's theorem for [[Harmonic function|harmonic functions]], or solutions to [[Laplace's equation]]. It states that bounded harmonic functions in Euclidean space are constant. [[Edward Nelson]] gave a short proof in 1961, exploiting the mean-value property of harmonic functions.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Edward|last=Nelson|title=A proof of Liouville's theorem|journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]|year=1961|volume=12|issue=6|pages=995|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1961-0259149-4|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Mathematical physics ===
Since the middle eighteenth century, mathematicians and physicists had been studying a variety of [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] with [[Boundary value problem|boundary values]] using the [[Separation of variables#Partial differential equations|separation of variables]] to resolve them into systems ordinary differential equations, which carried their own parameters. Solutions found for specific values of these parameters, called [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]], were known as [[Eigenfunction|eigenfunctions]]. The separation of variables in different coordinate systems led to new special functions, such as the [[Bessel function|Bessel functions]] and [[Legendre polynomials]], as eigenfunctions of ordinary differential equations.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Kline |first=Morris |author-link=Morris Kline |title=Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1972 |isbn=0-19-506136-5 |pages= |chapter=}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=715}} Liouville and his friend, [[Jacques Charles François Sturm]], sought to tackle the general problem for any linear differential equations of the second order. In a series papers published in the 1830s, the two men established the [[Sturm–Liouville theory]].<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|pages=715-6}} Though the significance of this contribution took some time for mathematicians to grasp,<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |author-link=Carl Benjamin Boyer |title=A History of Mathematics |last2=Merzbach |first2=Uta |author-link2=Uta Merzbach |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=1991 |isbn=0-471-09763-2 |edition=2nd |location=New York}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=571}} it is now a standard procedure to solve certain types of [[integral equation]]s.<ref name=":2" /> Their work was inspired by the analysis of [[Heat equation|heat diffusion]] in a cylinder by [[Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier]],<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Grattan-Guinness |first=Ivor |author-link=Ivor Grattan-Guinness |date=May 1973 |title=More Recent Mathematics: ''Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times'', Morris Kline |url=https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.180.4086.627 |journal=Science |volume=180 |issue=4086 |pages=627-8 |doi=10.1126/science.180.4086.627|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and may be viewed as a generalization of [[Fourier analysis]].<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=571}} In its original formulation, the Sturm–Liouville theory was not fully rigorous in that it did not adequately address the completeness of the set of eigenfunctions (or [[Orthogonal basis|orthogonal basis set)]] and the convergence of the expansion in terms of the eigenfunctions.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=717}} These issues were subsequently addressed by mathematicians such as [[Maxime Bôcher]], [[Max Mason]], and [[Garrett Birkhoff]].<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=572}} 

Independent of [[Niels Henrik Abel]], Liouville studied special integral equations and employed [[Liouville–Neumann series|a method of successive substitutions]], anticipating [[Carl Neumann]] by a few decades. However, his contributions in this domain were subsequently subsumed by the work of [[Vito Volterra]], a pioneer of the general theory of integral equations.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=1054}} Liouville's research on the Sturm–Liouville theory and linear integral equations constituted early advances in the study of [[functional analysis]].<ref name=":5" />  

In 1837,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Liouville |first=Joseph |date=1837 |title=Sur le développement des fonctions et séries |journal=Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées |volume=1 |pages=16–35}}</ref> Liouville sought approximate solutions to linear second-order differential equations with spatially varying coefficients and obtained, in modern language, an [[Asymptotic expansion|asymptotic series]].<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=1101}} [[George Green (mathematician)|George Green]] independently found this technique in the same year in a paper on water waves in a canal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Green |first=George |date=1837 |title=On the motion of waves in a variable canal of small depth and width |journal=Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society |volume=6 |pages=457–62}}</ref> The [[WKB approximation|Liouville–Green method]] was rediscovered in 1923 by [[Harold Jeffreys]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jeffreys |first=Harold |date=1923 |title=On Certain Approximate Solutions of Linear Differential Equations of the Second Order |url=https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/plms/s2-23.1.428 |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |volume=s2-23 |pages=428-436 |doi=10.1112/plms/s2-23.1.428|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and again in 1926 by [[Gregor Wentzel]], [[Hans Kramers]], [[Léon Brillouin]], who were studying the [[Schrödinger equation]] of quantum mechanics.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=1101}}
[[File:Simple Harmonic Motion Orbit.gif|thumb|An animation illustrating Liouville's theorem for [[simple harmonic motion]]. The area of the phase-space portrait is constant.]]
Liouville was attracted to the study of mechanics thanks to the works of [[William Rowan Hamilton]] and [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]].<ref name=":5" /> Liouville proved in a 1838 paper on differential equations<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Liouville |first=Joseph |year=1838 |title=Sur la Theorie de la Variation des constantes arbitraires |url=http://sites.mathdoc.fr/JMPA/PDF/JMPA_1838_1_3_A26_0.pdf |journal=Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées |volume=3 |pages=342–349}}</ref> that [[phase space]] volume of a conservative mechanical system constant, a result now known as [[Liouville's theorem (Hamiltonian)|Liouville's theorem]] in [[Hamiltonian mechanics]].<ref name=":0" /> Following [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]], Liouville's theorem is recognized  a fundamental result for statistical mechanics.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tolman |first=Richard C. |author-link=Richard C. Tolman |title=The Principles of Statistical Mechanics |publisher=Dover Publications |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-486-63896-6 |orig-year=1938}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=48-51}} In a related context, Liouville introduced the notion of [[action-angle coordinates]] as a description of completely [[integrable systems]]. The modern formulation of this is sometimes called the [[Liouville–Arnold theorem]], and the underlying concept of integrability is referred to as Liouville integrability. 

In his study of electrodynamics, Liouville developed the [[Riemann–Liouville integral]] to consider differentiation and integration of a [[Fractional calculus|fractional order]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lützen |first=Jesper |author-link=Jesper Lützen |date=1985 |title=Liouville’s differential calculus of arbitrary order and its electrodynamical origin |journal=Proceedings of the 19th Nordic Congress Mathematicians |publisher=Icelandic Mathematical Society |pages=149–160}}</ref>

He also studied [[potential theory]]<ref name=":0" /> and ellipsoidal figures of equilibrium, including those of unequal axes, that is, [[Jacobi ellipsoid|Jacobi ellipsoids]].<ref name=":5" />

His unpublished manuscripts indicated that he had already known of the [[Rayleigh–Ritz method]] for approximating the eigenvalues of a [[Boundary value problem|boundary-value problem]] as early as 1845, decades before William Strutt ([[Lord Rayleigh]]) introduced it his ''Theory of Sound'' (1877).<ref name=":0" />

== Honours and awards ==
The crater [[Liouville (crater)|Liouville]] on the [[Moon]] is named after him.
